The pool of 585 to 908 events is mostly minor-league players who are not realistic MLB contributors. The design admits it avoids the minor/MLB separation, so the ranking may mostly sort obvious cases, such as players with recent MLB time, that every club already knows.

The outcome (≥50 PA or ≥20 IP in Y+1, any club) mostly measures opportunity. It depends on which club signs the player, its roster holes, and injuries. The design itself concedes this, so a model that predicts "who gets chances" can look useful without identifying under-evaluated talent.

B0 ranks by MLB playing time in Y, and that is nearly the same signal as the outcome (persistence of MLB roles). M includes the same variable, so M beating B0 may only reflect fitting the opportunity signal. A positive result would show persistence, not value found.

B1 may be a weak or poorly specified baseline. Ranking by level and then OPS or K-BB% ignores park, league, and sample size, and level-specific rates are not comparable across Triple-A run environments. Beating a strawman is easy. A fairer baseline would be M's own features with hand-set weights, or a public projection system if it was published before the decision date.
Selecting the stronger of B0/B1 on the 2024 validation cohort, a single season, is noisy. The "stronger baseline" label may be chosen by chance.

Hindsight and leakage risk is not closed. "Highest level reached in Y" and season-Y stats retrieved later may include late-season corrections. Age is defined at Dec 31. Players whose release or election timing reflects information about the next season are another risk. The decision-date availability of each field is not verified. Players who re-sign with the same club also create selection effects.
Treating the same player in several cohorts as separate decisions inflates effective sample size and may leak across the temporal split. The design reports the overlap but sets no limit on it.
The 2019 cohort's outcome season is 2020. Scaling by 60/162 changes the threshold and the opportunity structure, so it is not comparable with other cohorts. Treat it as sensitivity only.

k=50 is justified only by a reference to a typical club's offer count, which is unchecked. A fixed k for the whole league may not match the Cubs' actual contract and NRI counts. A club that signs 50 players may already include its own re-signings.

The +3 hits threshold has no power analysis. If the base rate is around 10% and the top 50 holds 10 to 20 positives, the sampling noise of a difference of 3 is large with one holdout cohort. The paired bootstrap over players ignores cohort-level and club-level dependence, so the intervals will be too narrow. Passing the threshold could be noise.
The stop rule (<15 positives per cohort) is too lax. Even 15 positives would leave top-50 differences uninformative.

Existing public tools may already cover this: MLB Pipeline and transaction trackers, MiLB free-agent lists, public projection systems, and farm-system ranking sites. The design does not survey them and does not compare against any of them.

Looking useful without advantage is the main risk. Examples: (1) AUROC and calibration can be good because of easy negatives, such as 30-year-old players with no upper-level time, while the top-50 decision is unchanged. (2) Using the "any club" outcome credits the model for the signing club's choices. (3) The Cubs retrospective compares to signings the Cubs made and then reports "what the method would have flagged," which cannot show improvement and invites storytelling from a few anecdotes. (4) Several secondary metrics and a validation tuning step give room for a favorable story. (5) A model that mostly re-ranks players clubs would sign anyway can show high hits while adding no incremental player over the club's own picks.

Define the primary metric as incremental hits among players NOT already obvious: exclude players with MLB time in Y or Y-1 from the top-k, or stratify by that, so the test addresses the low-attention segment the design says matters.
Add a stronger baseline set: B2, M's features with hand-set weights, and a pre-decision public projection if archived. Fix B0/B1 choice from pooled prior cohorts, not a single validation year.

Replace the opportunity-dependent outcome with, or add, a performance-conditional outcome (e.g., value per PA given playing time above a threshold), and report results conditional on signing club's role to separate talent from chance.

Run a power simulation before the holdout using the training cohorts. Use a cohort-level block bootstrap or leave-one-cohort-out, pre-register k at several values (25, 50, 100), and set the threshold from the simulated noise, not an intuitive +3.
Add a null check: shuffle outcomes within strata of age and level to show what hit counts a stratum-only ranking gives, and a freeze-and-timestamp audit of every feature's availability date.

The November decision may not change with a ranking. Most of the several hundred electors are low-level minor leaguers a club would never pursue, and clubs likely already shortlist from internal reports, so a whole-pool ranking may only reorder players that staff would have reviewed anyway.

The outcome (>=50 PA or >=20 IP) mostly measures opportunity. It depends on the signing club's roster holes, injuries, and 40-man status, so it can reward models that predict who gets chances (age, MLB time in Y) rather than who is good. A rate-based or WAR-above-replacement-style outcome, or a regression on playing time, would separate the two.

Prior MLB playing time is both a feature and a near-proxy for the outcome, so M may beat B1 simply by rediscovering B0. B1 omits MLB playing time, which makes it a weakened comparator. The design says the better of B0/B1 is the benchmark, but a stronger baseline (B0 and B1 combined, or a logistic regression on only 2-3 features) is missing.

Public tools already cover parts of this: public projection systems, minor-league leaderboards, transaction trackers, and prospect-ranking sites. The design lists no comparison against them, so any win over weak baselines may say nothing about added value.

Leakage risk: the "elected free agency" event can embed selection (players the club chose not to retain), and the Dec 31 availability cutoff is hard to verify for stats that get revised or for retroactively corrected transaction records. Players repeating across cohorts also carry label-correlated history into training and holdout.

Hindsight risk: the 2025 holdout is described as uninspected, but the designers know the pool size and the 2026 season is finished. Cohort definitions, k, and the +3 threshold were set by people who may know aggregate base rates, so the pre-registration is only partially blind.

k=50 is justified only by a hypothesis about club signing volume that is unchecked. A club does not choose from a fixed 50, and the pool has a large share of already-ineligible or unreachable players. Top-50 hits could also be dominated by players with recent MLB time who were never gettable cheaply.

The +3 hits threshold has no derivation from variance, the base rate, or the value of a depth player. With a single holdout cohort and possibly 15-60 positives, bootstrap noise on top-50 counts may be about as large as 3. Passing could be luck, and failing could hide a real gain.

Cohort-level sample size is small: roughly six training cohorts and one holdout, with correlated players across years. The design's early-stop at <15 positives per cohort is low, since a top-50 comparison at that level is almost uninformative.

The pool is uncertain because the minor-league versus MLB election split is unresolved (113 players apart in 2018). Using the whole pool avoids that issue, but mixes populations with very different base rates, so AUROC may look strong from easy separation (MLB veterans vs. A-ball players) while top-50 within the relevant segment shows nothing.

The project would look useful but give little advantage if: AUROC is high due to easy cases; hits are driven by players who re-sign quickly with their own club; the headline metric counts players clubs could not acquire; the Cubs retrospective is read as validation; or the model is compared to nothing a real scout uses. Private club data would likely already cover the same ground.

Dropping 2020 and scaling the 2019 cohort's threshold by 60/162 introduces arbitrary choices that can be tuned after the fact. The 2021 cohort follows a disrupted minor-league return and may differ in structure.
Source terms limit use to individual, non-commercial, non-bulk, which may conflict with building multi-year cohort tables across hundreds of players per year.

Replace the single +3 rule with a pre-registered threshold derived from a simulation of bootstrap variance on the validation cohort, and report effect sizes across all cohorts via rolling-origin evaluation instead of one holdout.

Stratify the pool before ranking (prior MLB time vs. none, pitcher vs. hitter), evaluate top-k within the no-MLB stratum, and use a rate-based or above-replacement outcome alongside the playing-time threshold.

Add stronger baselines: B0+B1 combined, last-year-stats-only logistic, and a public projection system, plus a "tops by age only" null. Report an opportunity-adjusted outcome that conditions on the signing club's roster openings where public.
Choose k from measured public signing counts (Cubs and other clubs) before looking at any holdout outcomes, and show a sweep over k=25/50/100 with intervals.

The design avoids the S1 separation conflict by ranking the whole pool, but that makes the pool include players the decision-maker would never pursue (MLB-service-time veterans, 6-year minor-league free agents, players already agreed to re-sign). Top-50 hits may then be dominated by obvious MLB-experienced players, which B0 already ranks highly; M's lead over B0 could come from re-discovering "had MLB time in Y" rather than finding anything a scout would not already see.

The November decision may not change with a ranking. Clubs already have internal lists, and the best players sign within days, often with the club that holds their rights or on terms agreed before the pool opens. The design provides no evidence that a club's actual choice set at decision time resembles the full elected-free-agency list.

The outcome (>=50 PA or >=20 IP in Y+1) measures opportunity at least as much as value. A player who signs with a team lacking depth reaches 50 PA through roster need, and a good player blocked on a deep roster does not. The design admits this bias but proposes no correction. It would also reward predicting "who gets a 40-man spot", which can be learned from MLB time and level alone.

Add a value-conditioned secondary outcome (e.g., WAR or runs above replacement per PA/IP, with a minimum-opportunity gate) and a opportunity-adjusted outcome (e.g., stratify by signing club's depth-chart slot), and report both beside the binary threshold.

The 50 PA / 20 IP threshold is arbitrary and treats a 20 IP reliever and a 50 PA bench bat as equal. Pitchers and hitters likely have very different base rates, so a pooled top-50 may be mostly one group depending on the ranking.
Rank and evaluate hitters and pitchers separately, or fix a quota (e.g., 25/25), and run a sensitivity analysis on thresholds fixed before the holdout.

Hindsight risk in the 2025 holdout. The design was written 2026-10-09 after the 2026 season ended and after the 2025 cohort pool size was seen. Anyone who knows 2026 outcomes, including the authors from general baseball knowledge, could shape features, baselines, or k. The statement "not inspected for outcomes" is unverified and is not independently checkable.

Pre-register by hashing the frozen code and config before retrieving any 2026 outcomes, and prefer a purely historical blinded check (e.g., rerun on 2018 to 2024 with rolling-origin splits) so the conclusion does not rest on one cohort.

Leakage risk through "highest level reached in Y" and "MLB playing time in Y". Transactions dated through Dec 31 mean the feature window includes events after election (e.g., minor-league deals signed in December), and the elected free agency event type itself may leak information (e.g., players who elect after being outrighted have different histories than players released). Age at Dec 31 and as-of dates must be checked per event.

The multi-cohort split is nearly a one-sample test. Only one holdout cohort of about 839 players exists, and the same players recur across cohorts (acknowledged, not quantified). The 2019 to 2020 cohort with a 60-game scaled threshold and the missing 2020 cohort leave only about five clean training years, with a COVID shift in roster behavior.

Base rate risk cuts both ways. If the base rate is around 10 to 20 percent of about 800 players, the top-50 count has a standard error of a few players, so a +3 threshold is about one standard deviation of sampling noise from a single cohort. A bootstrap on one cohort captures player sampling but not season-to-season variation (injury luck, club needs), so the interval is too narrow for generalization.

The base rate of 0.15 in the CALC above is an illustrative placeholder, not a measured value. The stopping rule (<15 positives per cohort) is so lax that it will almost never trigger and does not guarantee the top-50 comparison is informative.

k=50 is justified only by an unchecked statement about club signing volume. Clubs sign minor-league deals for many reasons (org depth for affiliates) that don't aim at MLB contribution. The +3 hits threshold has a rationale ("scout-level noise") with no data. A top-50 hit gain of 3 on a base of maybe 20 hits is roughly 15 percent relative; on a base of 10 hits, 30 percent. Neither is tied to wins or cost.

Replace the fixed +3 with a threshold derived from a decision model: value of an additional usable depth player in runs or dollars versus scout time, and report results for several k (25, 50, 100) with a fixed ordering of primary versus secondary before the holdout.

Baselines B0 and B1 may be weak or unfair in either direction. B0 uses MLB playing time and is a strong proxy for the outcome, since the same players tend to get MLB time again. B1 uses OPS and K-BB% across levels without park, league, or age-relative-to-level adjustments, so it is a straw man for hitters at Triple-A versus Double-A. M gets to learn age-by-level interactions via regression while the baselines have none. Choosing the better baseline on a single validation cohort (2024) is itself noisy.

Add stronger comparators: persistence (Y+1 outcome equals Y outcome), a plain age-and-level-only model, and any public projection systems (e.g., public aggregated projections for MLB-experienced players), and test M against the best of these on the holdout.

Existing public resources already approximate this: public transaction trackers and free-agent lists, prospect and minor-league leaderboards, public projection systems, and club-agnostic fan analyses of minor-league free agents. I have not verified which are current or how good they are. If these already give the same ranking, the project gives parity, not an edge, and clubs with private tracking data and scouting reports start from a better information set.

What would make this LOOK useful while providing little advantage: (1) M beats B0/B1 mainly because of MLB-time and level features that any scout reads off a transactions page; (2) the binary outcome rewards opportunity, not talent; (3) a clean-looking bootstrap interval from one cohort; (4) the Cubs retrospective compares to signings already made without knowing alternatives, offers, or competing bids; (5) high AUROC across a pool where most players are trivially low-probability; (6) retrospective examples of "players the Cubs missed" selected after outcomes are known; (7) no cost or availability constraint.

Report AUROC and precision restricted to the plausibly actionable segment (players with no MLB service-time lock, not already re-signed within a few days), plus a "what did M add beyond B0 and public projections" incremental-value test, and require the lift to survive in the "no MLB in Y" segment, where the claimed edge for neglected players should live.

The feasibility evidence covers only event counts and API availability. It does not show that features such as season-Y stats by level, Y+1 outcomes, or as-of timing are obtainable within the stated source terms (individual, non-commercial, non-bulk use) or the 3 remaining sessions. The design's reliance on bulk cohort construction may conflict with those terms.

Rule 5 codes appear only from 2024, and the design's own Cubs case requires comparing against public signings that are hard to link to the DFA-type events reliably. Name matching between transaction records and stats IDs is an untested error source.

The right verdict if only the headline holds: a positive result would show retrospective rankability, not an actionable advantage. A negative result is more informative and the design's COMPLETE_NEGATIVE rule is sound, but the design should state that a positive result alone does not justify a Cubs recommendation without availability, cost, and incremental-value tests.
